meta.title: Who really said "The Buck Stops Here"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Truman had the sign, but not the words. An anonymous Army lieutenant had the motto above his desk in 1929 — sixteen years earlier.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Buck Stops Here'?
meta.ogDescription: Truman popularized it; he didn’t coin it. The motto was on an unnamed lieutenant’s desk card by October 1929.

answer.label: Not Harry Truman — an anonymous Army desk motto
answer.authorDates: First in print 2 October 1929 · the officer who used it was never named
answer.sourceLine: The sign on Truman’s desk is real, and so is his ownership of the idea — but the words were already circulating when he got them. Quote Investigator’s earliest match ↗ is a newspaper column from 2 October 1929, sixteen years before Truman became president, describing a card above a second lieutenant’s desk in the war department: “The buck stops here” — “and he didn’t mean buck private.” The officer is not named, and QI’s verdict is that “the creator of the expression remains unknown”. Between 1929 and 1945 QI finds the motto on at least four more desks — a brigadier general’s, two captains’, and the governor of Wyoming’s — before any reporter saw one on Truman’s, in January 1946. What Truman did was make it famous.

source.excerpt: Capt. Joe Lehman tells a story that Jug should bear. . . . It’s about the second lieutenant in the war department whose desk was back in the corner among the boxes and barrels. . . . Above this desk the second looey had placed a card which read: “The buck stops here” . . . and he didn’t mean buck private.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ states the conclusion in its own words: “the motto appeared on the desk of a U.S. military officer in 1929, but the officer was unnamed, and the creator of the expression remains unknown.” Its earliest citation is The Lincoln Evening Journal, 2 October 1929, “I May Be Wrong” by John Bentley, quote page 13, column 1, Lincoln, Nebraska — a citation QI credits to researcher Barry Popik.

The motto then turns up on desk after desk, all before Truman’s. QI documents Brigadier General A. B. Warfield citing it at a laundry managers’ meeting in Hospital Management, October 1939 (verified from scans via the University of Georgia library system), and again in a Reno Evening Gazette photo caption of 1 October 1942; Capt. Spencer Z. Hilliard’s office at Baraboo, Wisconsin in the Wisconsin State Journal of 26 April 1942; and Capt. Clifford M. Alexander in an Associated Press story of 25 November 1943.

It had even reached a state governor first. QI cites a United Press filler of 19 September 1945 headed “NO BUCK PASSER”: “Gov. Lester C. Hunt has a neatly lettered sign on his desk reading: ‘The Buck Stops Here.’” That is weeks before any reporter describes one on Truman’s desk.

Truman’s own sign enters the record in January 1946, in an International News Service piece by Bob Considine (Buffalo Courier-Express, 23 January 1946, page 3): “He has one neatly lettered desk sign reading, ‘The Buck Stops Here.’” QI’s summary is that Truman “did place a sign on his desk… by 1946” and “also mentioned the saying in his speeches, but the motto was already in circulation.”

Wikiquote files the line under Misattributed on its Truman page ↗: “This saying, also popularized by Truman, was on a sign on his desk, but did not originate with him. According to the Truman Presidential Library, it was sent to him nearly two months after the Hiroshima atomic bombing.” That dating is reported here as Wikiquote gives it; the Truman Library’s own site could not be reached from this session to check it directly.

Wikipedia’s article on buck passing ↗ agrees that the phrase “was popularized by U.S. President Harry S. Truman” rather than coined by him, says he received the sign “as a gift from a prison warden who was also an avid poker player”, and traces the underlying idiom to poker, where “a marker or counter (such as a knife with a buckhorn handle during the American Frontier era) was used to indicate the person whose turn it was to deal”.
source.excerptNote: The 1929 column as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗; the ellipses are in the original, and “second looey” is period slang for a second lieutenant. The joke in the last clause is the part that gets lost: a “buck private” is the lowest rank, so the lieutenant is saying that the responsibility stops with him and also that he is nobody’s dogsbody. Nothing in the column suggests the officer invented the line either — it is simply the first time anyone wrote it down.

source.rightsNote: Public domain in the United States. The earliest documented appearance is a newspaper column of 2 October 1929 — comfortably before the 1931 cutoff — and the motto was anonymous and in common circulation before that. There is no identifiable author or estate to hold a right in it, and a four-word desk slogan is in any case about as far from a protectable work as writing gets. Use it freely.

author.name: Harry S. Truman
author.kicker: The man who got the credit
author.heading: So why Truman?
author.bio: Harry S. Truman (8 May 1884 – 26 December 1972) became president in April 1945 on Franklin Roosevelt’s death and served until 1953, deciding to use the atomic bomb, recognising Israel, desegregating the armed forces and committing American troops to Korea. He was a Missouri haberdasher and county judge before the Senate, had no college degree, and was not expected to be any good at the job. The sign suited him because the defining feature of his presidency was taking decisions nobody else could be blamed for — which is why a motto that had spent sixteen years on the desks of army adjutants stuck permanently to him instead.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Nobody is being smeared here: Truman really did keep the sign, really did mean it, and really did make the phrase part of the language. The error is narrower and more common than outright invention — crediting the popularizer with the coinage.

items.why: The sign was on his Oval Office desk and reporters wrote about it from January 1946 onward, so the association is earned. But QI finds the motto in print in 1929 ↗ and on four other men’s desks before his, and concludes the motto “was already in circulation”. Wikiquote lists it among his misattributed quotations ↗ for exactly this reason.

QI is explicit that the 1929 lieutenant is the earliest user found, not the author: he is unnamed, and “the creator of the expression remains unknown”. This page therefore credits no one. Any source that hands you a named inventor for this phrase is going beyond the evidence that exists.

Wikipedia says “the reverse of the sign reads, ‘I’m from Missouri’” ↗, making it one two-sided object. The contemporary 1946 report QI quotes describes them as separate items on the desk — “Another says, with some meaning, ‘I’m From Missouri’” — alongside a third adjustable gadget reading “No”, “Yes” or “Scram”. Both accounts are reported here; neither is adopted, and the Truman Library, which holds the artefact, was unreachable from this session.

misattribution.truthLine: QI’s verdict ↗: an anonymous US military desk motto, documented in October 1929 and passed from desk to desk for sixteen years before it reached Truman’s. He gave it a presidency to sit in; he did not write it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The phrase only works if you know the one it answers. To “pass the buck” comes from poker, where a marker — by tradition a knife with a buckhorn handle — sat in front of whoever had to deal, and could be pushed along to duck the job. “The buck stops here” is therefore not a boast about power. It is a refusal to push the marker, which is why it kept appearing on the desks of adjutants and quartermasters: the people everything unwanted rolls downhill toward.

A Wisconsin State Journal reporter caught that tone exactly in 1944, writing of one such adjutant: “It probably was correct, and all the unwanted tasks from higher up that could be passed on eventually reached him.” Truman’s version inverted the joke. On a president’s desk the same four words stop being gallows humour about being at the bottom and become a statement about being at the top — and that is the reading the phrase has carried ever since.
detailsBody: The sixteen-year trail QI assembles is the most convincing part of the case, because it is not one stray citation but a pattern. 1929: an unnamed second lieutenant, desk wedged among boxes and barrels. 1939: Brigadier General A. B. Warfield invoking the motto in a talk on co-operation, to an audience of hospital laundry managers. 1942: Captain Spencer Z. Hilliard at Baraboo, and Warfield again in a Reno photo caption. 1943: Captain Clifford M. Alexander, in an AP story about a man who built a prisoner-of-war camp in a day. September 1945: the governor of Wyoming. Only then, in January 1946, does a reporter find one on the president’s desk.

Two honest limits on this page. First, nothing here establishes that the 1929 lieutenant coined the phrase — he is simply the earliest person documented using it, and QI says so. Second, the circumstances of Truman’s own sign are reported at second hand: the Truman Presidential Library’s website is not reachable from this session, so the dating “nearly two months after the Hiroshima atomic bombing” is given as Wikiquote’s citation of the Library rather than as something checked at source, and the donor appears here only as Wikipedia describes him, a poker-playing prison warden, because no source read for this page names him.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI concludes: 'the motto appeared on the desk of a U.S. military officer in 1929, but the officer was unnamed, and the creator of the expression remains unknown.' It adds that Truman placed the sign on his desk by 1946 and mentioned the saying in speeches, 'but the motto was already in circulation.'

QI's earliest match is The Lincoln Evening Journal, 2 October 1929, 'I May Be Wrong' by John Bentley, quote page 13 column 1, Lincoln, Nebraska, reading: 'Above this desk the second looey had placed a card which read: "The buck stops here" . . . and he didn't mean buck private.' QI credits the citation to researcher Barry Popik.

QI documents pre-Truman users: Brig. Gen. A. B. Warfield in Hospital Management, October 1939 (verified with scans via the University of Georgia library system) and a Reno Evening Gazette photo caption of 1 October 1942; Capt. Spencer Z. Hilliard, Wisconsin State Journal, 26 April 1942; Capt. Clifford M. Alexander, Associated Press, 25 November 1943; and Gov. Lester C. Hunt of Wyoming, United Press, 19 September 1945.

QI's first report of Truman's sign is Bob Considine (International News Service), Buffalo Courier-Express, 23 January 1946, page 3 column 2: 'He has one neatly lettered desk sign reading, "The Buck Stops Here." Another says, with some meaning, "I'm From Missouri." An intricate one which can be adjusted three ways reads "No," or "Yes" or "Scram."'

Wikiquote's Harry S. Truman page lists 'The buck stops here!' under Misattributed, stating it 'was on a sign on his desk, but did not originate with him' and that according to the Truman Presidential Library it was sent to him nearly two months after the Hiroshima atomic bombing.

Wikipedia states the phrase 'was popularized by U.S. President Harry S. Truman', that he received the sign as a gift from a prison warden who was an avid poker player, that the reverse of the sign reads 'I'm from Missouri', and that 'pass the buck' originated in poker where a marker such as a knife with a buckhorn handle indicated whose turn it was to deal.
Harry S. Truman was born 8 May 1884 and died 26 December 1972, and was the 33rd President of the United States.
Lester Callaway Hunt Sr. (8 July 1892 - 19 June 1954) was an American Democratic politician from Wyoming.
